title: Develop own ability to provide a business advisory service for SMMEs

lessons.title: The role and competencies of an SMME business adviser
lessons.html:
What a business adviser does

Extension officers increasingly advise farmers not only on production but also on running their farms as businesses. A business advisory service helps SMME owners make better decisions about markets, money, people and growth. Typical clients are smallholder livestock farmers, vegetable co-operatives, agro-processors and agricultural service providers.

The adviser is not the owner. You do not make decisions or run the business. You help the owner see their situation clearly, understand options and build their own capability. A good adviser leaves the client stronger and less dependent over time.

Core competencies

  • Business knowledge: financial statements, gross margins, cash flow budgets, costing and pricing, marketing, basic labour and tax compliance.
  • Sector knowledge: how value chains work for local commodities such as red meat, poultry, vegetables, grain or citrus, and who the role players are.
  • Diagnostic skills: gathering information, analysing it and identifying root causes.
  • Interpersonal skills: building trust, listening, questioning, explaining in plain language and in the client's preferred language.
  • Networking: knowing where to refer clients, for example to development finance institutions, the Land Bank, SEDA, commodity organisations, accountants or legal advisers.
  • Professional ethics: confidentiality, honesty, avoiding conflicts of interest and staying within your competence.

Self-assessment

Developing your ability starts with an honest self-assessment. Rate yourself on each competency, then ask a supervisor or colleague to rate you too. Compare the results. Look for gaps that most affect your clients. An extension officer with strong crop knowledge may find that cash flow budgeting is the main gap holding back their advice.

Record your findings. They are the starting point for your personal development plan.

lessons.title: Building a personal development plan
lessons.html:
Planning your growth as an adviser

A personal development plan (PDP) turns your self-assessment into action. It should be realistic, linked to the needs of your clients, and reviewed regularly with your supervisor.

Elements of a PDP

ElementExample
Development goalPrepare accurate 12-month cash flow budgets for livestock clients
Learning activitiesShort course in farm financial management; practise with three client cases; review by an agricultural economist
ResourcesCourse fee, spreadsheet templates, enterprise budgets from the provincial department
TimeframeComplete by end of the second quarter
EvidenceThree completed budgets checked and accepted by clients

Ways to learn

  • Formal learning: accredited short courses, diplomas, or unit standards in business advice and agricultural economics.
  • Learning on the job: working alongside an experienced adviser on real client assignments.
  • Mentoring and coaching: a regular conversation with an experienced practitioner who reviews your work.
  • Self-study: industry publications, commodity organisation reports, market price information and enterprise budgets.
  • Peer learning: study groups or case discussions with other extension officers.
  • Networking: attending farmer days, agribusiness forums and industry conferences.

Mix several methods. Courses give theory, but you build real skill by applying it to clients and reflecting on the results.

Review your PDP with your supervisor every quarter. Tick off completed goals, note what you learnt and set new goals as your client base changes, for example when you start working with agro-processors as well as primary producers.

Professional registration

Find out whether professional bodies relevant to your work offer registration and continuing professional development requirements. For extension practitioners, registration with the relevant professional body may be expected by employers. Check the current requirements with your employer, as they can change.

lessons.title: Delivering, reflecting and improving
lessons.html:
The advisory process in practice

Your ability as an adviser grows through practice. A clear process helps you deliver consistent service and learn from each assignment:

  1. Contracting: agree with the client what help is needed, what you will do, what they will do, timelines and confidentiality.
  2. Diagnosis: gather and analyse information about the business.
  3. Options and recommendations: present practical choices with costs and benefits in rand.
  4. Action planning: agree specific steps the owner will take, with dates.
  5. Follow-up: check progress, solve new problems and adjust the plan.
  6. Closure: review results with the client and close the assignment.

Reflective practice

After each assignment, reflect in writing. Ask yourself: what went well, what did not, what did I learn about the client and about myself, and what will I do differently? For example, you may notice that your report was too technical and the owner did not act on it. Next time you might present findings verbally with a one-page summary in the client's language.

Getting feedback

Ask clients for feedback through a short conversation or form: was the advice useful, practical and clear, and did they act on it? Ask your supervisor or mentor to review sample client files. Track results such as increased sales, improved record keeping or successful loan applications. Over time this gives you evidence of your impact.

Staying ethical and within competence

Never give advice beyond your competence, especially on legal, tax or complex financial matters. Refer the client to a qualified professional. Declare any conflict of interest, for example if a relative supplies inputs to the client. Keep client information confidential.

Update your PDP at least once a year based on reflection and feedback. Development as an adviser is continuous.

Key points

  • The adviser supports the owner's decisions and builds their capability, not dependence.
  • Assess your competencies honestly, with input from others.
  • Write a PDP with goals, activities, resources, timeframes and evidence.
  • Use a clear advisory process from contracting to closure.
  • Reflect after each assignment, seek feedback and refer matters beyond your competence.
